sections.h2: Where is Middlesex County, NJ, and what towns does it include?
sections.html:
Middlesex County sits in central New Jersey, running from the Raritan Valley toward the northern end of the Jersey Shore. Wikipedia reports 322.87 square miles in total, with 309.22 of them land, and describes a largely flat county bisected by the Raritan River. The county seat is New Brunswick, home of Rutgers University.

The county government counts twenty-five municipalities. Edison is the largest, with 107,588 residents in 2020, and Monroe Township covers the most ground at 42.19 square miles. Woodbridge Township holds the junction of the New Jersey Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway, and East Brunswick contains the state's center of population. Other towns include Perth Amboy, South Amboy, South Brunswick, Metuchen and South Plainfield.

Because the county is large and varied, a house in a Raritan Bay town such as South Amboy and one in a Route 1 corridor township such as South Brunswick are billed by different municipalities and school districts, even though the same county board rules on their appeals.

sections.h2: Which offices run property tax in Middlesex County?
sections.html:
Middlesex County does not send most homeowners a tax bill. In each of the twenty-five towns, a local assessor values property and a local collector sends the bill, and the county board of taxation supervises that work and hears appeals. Your town's collector is the person to ask for payment help and payoff numbers.

The Middlesex County Board of Taxation lists these basics:

  • Location: County Administration Building, 4th Floor, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick, NJ 08901.
  • Phone: 732-745-3350. The office opens weekdays from 8:30 AM until 4:15 PM.
  • Duties: certifying assessments and municipal tax rates, equalizing assessments for county taxes, preparing the abstract of ratables, supervising local assessors and hearing appeals.

The board explains that county tax boards were created by legislation in 1909 and that all 21 of them follow a uniform set of rules written by the state Division of Taxation. Five commissioners sit on the Middlesex board, and the county tax administrator runs the daily office.

sections.h2: What are the Middlesex County assessment appeal deadlines?
sections.html:
Regular appeals are due on or before April 1, or within 45 days after assessment notices are mailed in bulk, and May 1 applies where a town carried out a revaluation or reassessment. The state's guide to tax appeal hearings gives those dates, and Middlesex is not one of the three counties on the alternate calendar.

The county board adds several practical points:

  • Petitions can be filed through the board's online portal after creating an account, and the portal issues proof of filing.
  • The petition is forwarded to the board, the municipal assessor and the municipal clerk.
  • Evidence can be uploaded at filing or up to seven calendar days before the hearing, by 4:00 PM.
  • The deadline for added and omitted assessment appeals in 2026 was December 1.
  • The board resolved that it will not hold virtual tax appeal hearings.

An appeal covers the assessment only. The state guide notes that taxes come from local budgets and cannot be appealed, and it describes the common level range, which is plus or minus 15% of the director's ratio for the town. It also explains the freeze act, which holds an appealed value for the assessment year and the next two years unless something changes the property.

sections.h2: How does Middlesex County compare with its neighbors on housing and income?
sections.html:
Middlesex County is dense and diverse, and its home values trail those of neighboring Monmouth County. Census QuickFacts shows the following for the 2020-2024 survey period unless noted.

More than a third of Middlesex households rent, and the county reports 2,791.4 people per square mile. For sellers, that means a large pool of condominium and multifamily properties alongside single-family houses, and a lot of buyers who commute by rail or turnpike.

sections.h2: What is the land and climate like across Middlesex County?
sections.html:
The county is flat to gently rolling. Wikipedia puts elevations between sea level and about 300 feet, with the high ground near Route 1 in South Brunswick and a moraine ridge stretching through Perth Amboy, Woodbridge, Edison and Metuchen. Clay was mined along the Raritan Formation until the late twentieth century, especially near Woodbridge.

The climate is hot-summer humid continental, bordering humid subtropical along Raritan Bay and the Arthur Kill. New Brunswick averages 31.9 degrees Fahrenheit in January and 75.6 in July, and monthly precipitation runs from 2.98 inches in February to 5.08 inches in July. Wet summers and freezing winters are normal here, so roofs, gutters and basements are routine items on a buyer's inspection list.

sections.h2: Which employers and transport links shape the Middlesex County market?
sections.html:
The county's economy runs on health care, education, pharmaceuticals, finance and logistics. Wikipedia lists Rutgers University as the largest non-governmental employer, followed by Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital, and names Bristol-Myers Squibb, Wakefern Food Corporation, Johnson & Johnson, Prudential and several other hospitals among the large employers. The Bureau of Economic Analysis put the county's gross domestic product at $59.0 billion in 2021, second in New Jersey.

Transport matters just as much. Several stations on NJ Transit's Northeast Corridor Line serve the county, and the Turnpike and Parkway meet in Woodbridge. Census data puts the average commute at 31.2 minutes. Ask the assessor in your town how commute access is reflected in the value on your record.

sections.h2: What should a Middlesex County seller do about unpaid property tax?
sections.html:
Start with the collector in the municipality where the house stands, because the county does not collect. Ask for a written payoff through the expected closing date, and ask whether the town has sold a tax lien on the parcel. New Jersey law makes the owner responsible for the tax even without a bill, and quarterly due dates fall on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1 statewide.

If you plan to appeal, remember that the appeal must be filed by April 1 (May 1 after a revaluation), and that the first quarter's taxes and municipal charges are normally required to be paid for an appeal to proceed. Contact the county tax board at 732-745-3350 with questions about a pending petition, because the outcome can lower the value that a buyer sees on the record.

Relief programs also change with a sale. The state's relief page lists the Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ programs and notes that the deadline for the 2025 application was November 2, 2026.

faqs.q: Where do I file a property tax appeal in Middlesex County?
faqs.a: File with the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, which accepts petitions online and at 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. The board forwards each petition to the municipal assessor and clerk.

faqs.q: What is the standard appeal deadline in Middlesex County?
faqs.a: April 1, or within 45 days after bulk-mailed assessment notices, with May 1 for towns that completed a revaluation or reassessment. Added and omitted assessment appeals for 2026 were due December 1.

faqs.q: Does Middlesex County collect my property taxes?
faqs.a: No. Your municipal tax collector sends the bill and takes the payment, and the county board of taxation supervises assessments and hears appeals. Contact the collector in your town for a payoff figure.

faqs.q: How many municipalities are in Middlesex County?
faqs.a: There are twenty-five. They include Edison, Woodbridge, New Brunswick, East Brunswick, Monroe, Perth Amboy and South Brunswick, and each one runs its own assessment and collection offices.

faqs.q: Can I attend a Middlesex County tax appeal hearing by video?
faqs.a: No. The county board of taxation passed a resolution that it will not hold virtual tax appeal hearings, so plan to attend in person or send your evidence ahead of time.
